episodes.title: Lynching of Bill Young
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Bill Young was the hanging of a man by a mob at his home near Luray, Clark County, Missouri, on October 29, 1879, four days after a jury at Kahoka acquitted him of murdering the Spencer family. Wire reports carried the story nationally as a court verdict overturned by a mob, and the alleged leader, detective Frank Lane, was later indicted for murder but released on habeas corpus.

episodes.title: Lynching of Tom McDaniel
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Tom McDaniel took place on the night of August 31, 1880, when a band of men took McDaniel, a farmer of about 28, from his sickbed near Commercial Point, Pickaway County, Ohio, and hanged him to a tree near his home. A card on the body signed by a "Vigilance Committee" warned against interference, and an inquest returned a verdict of death by persons unknown. Papers across the country carried the story, many under the name Thomas McDonald, and a Columbus correspondent called it the first lynching in the county's history.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Bird
episodes.lead: The lynching of Henry Bird took place near Grayson, in Clinton County, Missouri, in late September 1880, when a search party of local men seized Bird, a Black farm laborer accused of raping his employer's wife, and he was hanged from an elm tree. The story ran as a wire item across the country, often misplaced in Kansas and once giving his name as "Henry Boyd", and a neighboring Missouri paper endorsed the killing.

episodes.title: Grant Parish seed-store shooting
episodes.lead: The Grant Parish seed-store shooting was a night attack in mid-September 1880 in which a party of unknown men fired into a cotton-seed store kept by Israel Smith, a Black man, about five miles south of Colfax, Louisiana, killing a boy of about 18 who was sleeping inside. The same party then fired into a second seed store owned by white men, wounding no one. The local Colfax Chronicle condemned the killing, and in December it linked the attackers to the burning of the same store.

episodes.title: Shooting of H. W. Wood
episodes.lead: The shooting of H. W. Wood was an ambush in Florida in late October 1880 in which unidentified men fired shotguns at Wood, the teacher of a colored school near Sorrento, and wounded him. The attack followed a written warning to stop teaching, and the Sanford Journal, whose report reached the Savannah Morning News, called for the attackers to be punished.

episodes.title: Whipping of a Fort Valley prisoner (1880)
episodes.lead: The whipping of a Fort Valley prisoner was an assault in Georgia in October 1880 in which unidentified men took a Black man accused of theft from a constable, whipped him to force a confession, and left him tied to a tree in front of the Fort Valley guardhouse. The episode reached the press only as the reported cause of a threat to burn Fort Valley, and the local paper that described it said its only evidence was the prisoner's own statement.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jose Francisco Gallegos and Thomas Valdez
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jose Francisco Gallegos and Thomas Valdez took place one night in October 1880 at Conejos, Colorado, when armed men took the two prisoners from the jail and hanged them from a nearby tree. The two men, described in the press as Mexicans, were awaiting trial for the murder of a traveler named S. Duprez, which they had reportedly confessed at a preliminary hearing in Albuquerque. Two New Mexico papers reported the lynching with approval, one under the headline "Retributive Justice."

episodes.title: Killing of William Arterberry
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The killing of William Arterberry was the shooting of a prisoner by a band of masked, armed men calling themselves "Vigilants" at Harrison, Boone County, Arkansas, on a Friday night in October 1880. Arterberry, suspected of setting fires in the town, was taken from the guards the sheriff had assigned him and shot dead. The local Harrison Times condemned the killing, and the story circulated in Arkansas papers and as far as Georgia.

episodes.title: Sale of Charles Green under the Colorado vagrancy law
episodes.lead: The sale of Charles Green under the Colorado vagrancy law took place in Leadville, Colorado, in late November 1880, when Green, a young Black man arrested as a vagrant, was auctioned off to labor for three months. The chief of police sold him for two dollars to C. E. Wyman, and a few days later Green was jailed on a theft charge and kept from his buyer. Papers in New Mexico and Indiana carried the story, the Indianapolis account presenting it as the return of something "old" under a new name.

episodes.title: Shooting of Dick Wilson
episodes.lead: The shooting of Dick Wilson was the wounding of a Black steamboat worker by Constable Wetherhorn on the streets of Savannah, Georgia, on the afternoon of November 16, 1880. Wilson, who had escaped from a magistrate's office while under arrest, was hit in the left leg by the fifth of five shots fired during a chase toward the Bay and was taken to jail. The Savannah Morning News, the only paper found to report it, noted that the shooting set off public discussion of officers firing at prisoners on city streets.

episodes.title: Alexandria third-ward polling violence
episodes.lead: The Alexandria third-ward polling violence took place on November 2, 1880, when Black Republican voters waiting at the court-house polls in Alexandria, Virginia, were crowded out, beaten and clubbed, and one was stabbed. Republican papers and witnesses blamed Democratic 'roughs' and Mayor Cortland Smith's police, while the Alexandria Gazette denied that any intimidation occurred. Republicans cited the episode as evidence against claims of peaceful Southern elections and threatened to contest the seat of the winning Democratic congressman, Barbour.

episodes.title: Threat against a Black federal marshal at Kingstree, 1880
episodes.lead: The threat against a Black federal marshal at Kingstree took place on election day, November 2, 1880, in Kingstree, Williamsburg County, South Carolina, when the state constable, Captain J. A. Kelley, announced that a colored U.S. marshal would be jailed if he tried to make any arrest. The marshal put away his badge and withdrew, and the day ended without reported violence, though a collision between white and Black residents was said to have been imminent. The account became known outside the state when a Washington Republican paper reprinted the local Kingstree Star's version under the heading "Red Shirt Tactics."

episodes.title: Disfranchisement of Black voters in the Richmond district, 1880
episodes.lead: The disfranchisement of Black voters in the Richmond district in 1880 was the exclusion, on election day, November 2, 1880, of voters in Virginia's Third Congressional District who had paid their poll tax to collectors appointed by the Readjuster State Auditor. Election judges rejected the receipts under an injunction issued the night before by Judge William Izard Clopton of Manchester, and a letter to the New-York Tribune alleged that men at the Richmond polls threatened Black voters with 'mob law' and tore up their receipts. Three Manchester election judges were indicted in federal court for refusing the votes of Black men.

episodes.title: Johnston's election-day shooting
episodes.lead: The Johnston's election-day shooting took place on November 2, 1880, at the polling place at Johnston's in Edgefield County, South Carolina, when men at the poll opened fire on a crowd of Black voters, killing one Black man and wounding several others. South Carolina papers blamed the Black voters, while national wires carried the killing as an 'election riot' at Edgefield with counts of the wounded that ranged from one to thirteen. Months later the killing was cited in a contested congressional election as evidence of Democratic violence that went unpunished.

episodes.title: Johnson's box election riot
episodes.lead: The Johnson's box election riot was a deadly clash at the Johnson's polling place in Edgefield County, South Carolina, on election day, November 2, 1880, in which one Black man was killed and several others were wounded. Election-night dispatches blamed Black voters for trying to seize the ballot-box, but evidence in a contested congressional election later said hundreds of Black Republicans had been kept from voting there and that no one had been tried for the killing.

episodes.title: Alleged election-day intimidation at Sumter, South Carolina (1880)
episodes.lead: The alleged election-day intimidation at Sumter, South Carolina, refers to reports on November 2, 1880, that armed Democrats crowded the polls in Sumter County, kept Republican voters away, and ejected federal deputy marshals. A private despatch to Senator Blaine went further, describing a riot and smashed ballot boxes, while dispatches to South Carolina papers said the election passed off quietly. No deaths or injuries were reported, and the dispute continued in Samuel Lee's contest of the First District congressional seat.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Jimmy Gates
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Jimmy Gates took place at Boise City, Idaho Territory, on November 28, 1880, when a large crowd surrounded Gates, accused of stabbing a packer, and threatened to hang him. Officers got him to jail with difficulty, and Pacific Coast papers carried the story as a short telegraphic item. No paper gives the race of Gates or of the wounded man.

episodes.title: Hanging of Herb Crater
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The hanging of Herb Crater was a nonfatal hanging in the autumn of 1880, reported from Wamega, Kansas, in which a group of masked men took Crater from jail at night and hung him from the joists of an opera house. Crater said the men wanted him to tell what he knew about horse thieving and let him live when he would not, and the only report of the episode is a short Wamega Tribune item reprinted in the Topeka Tribune.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of J. A. Hogan
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of J. A. Hogan took place at Central City, in the Black Hills of Dakota Territory, on the morning of November 23, 1880, when a mob went after Hogan, who had just shot a miner named Dan Falvey, intending to lynch him. The mob finally surrendered Hogan to the sheriff, and he was later tried for murder and found guilty of manslaughter after Falvey died. A Deadwood dispatch carried the episode to papers from Chicago to Los Angeles, some under headlines such as "Almost a Lynching"; none of the reports states the race of anyone involved.

episodes.title: Mobbing of Jack Minnicken
episodes.lead: The mobbing of Jack Minnicken was an attack on a Black Democratic voter, who was "set upon and mobbed" off the grounds of a Black camp meeting in early November 1880, in a place the report did not name, likely near Orangeburg, South Carolina, where it was printed. The Orangeburg Democrat, the only paper found to report it, said he was attacked for voting the Democratic ticket and tied it to a threat to shoot a second Black Democrat at the same meeting.

episodes.title: Lynching of Thornhill and Fields
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Thornhill and Fields was the killing of two men accused of horse-stealing, who were taken from the parish jail at Many, Sabine Parish, Louisiana, by armed men on a Thursday night in November 1880 and shot to death. A coroner's jury failed to identify the killers, and the case drew a brief editorial rebuke from Louisiana papers that said such killings were common in the parish.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Merrick Woodworth
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Merrick Woodworth was a threatened lynching at Pueblo, Colorado, on November 1, 1880, of a 50-year-old man accused of being found in bed with his daughter. Woodworth was reported to have narrowly escaped, and the episode is known only from a one-line telegram reprinted in four Western and Midwestern papers.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Peter Moore
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Peter Moore took place at Hempstead, Texas, in November 1880, after Moore, a Black man, was accused of shooting and killing City Marshal J. H. Adams. Threats of hanging led a deputy sheriff to move Moore to the jail at Brenham for safekeeping, and a Minnesota paper reported that a vigilance committee had formed and his lynching was expected. No attack on Moore was reported; he was tried at Hempstead in April 1881 and sentenced to seven years for second-degree murder.

episodes.title: Mob assault on Pettibone in Mobile
episodes.lead: The mob assault on Pettibone took place in Mobile, Alabama, on a Sunday evening in November 1880, probably November 21, when a large crowd roughly handled a Black man named Pettibone after his arrest and talked of lynching him. He and a second Black man had been arrested, accused of stopping two "young ladies" on the street; no killing was reported, and the episode is known from a single Alabama news brief.

episodes.title: Red Shirt seizure of the Darlington polls (1880)
episodes.lead: The Red Shirt seizure of the Darlington polls was the occupation of Darlington, South Carolina, by armed Red-Shirt Democrats on the night of November 1, 1880, and their control of the court-house polls on election day, November 2. According to a Darlington dispatch, Republicans who tried to vote had revolvers pointed at their heads, and a thousand or more were kept from voting. Northern Republican papers reported it as one of the frauds by which South Carolina was carried for Hancock.

episodes.title: Shooting of George Whittaker
episodes.lead: The shooting of George Whittaker took place on the night of November 3, 1880, in Frankfort, Kentucky, when Frank Egbert, a young white man, shot Whittaker, a Black boy who was cheering for James A. Garfield during a Republican celebration of the presidential election. Whittaker was wounded in the side and was not expected to recover, and Egbert was later held to the Circuit Court on a $500 bond. Wire summaries bundled the shooting with the accidental wounding of a Frankfort policeman the same night under headlines about pistols and political violence in Kentucky.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Emanuel Johnson
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Emanuel Johnson took place in Maury County, Tennessee, in November 1880, after Johnson, a Black railroad section hand, was accused of shooting and killing his white foreman, John Booth, who had discharged him. Newspapers predicted that Johnson would be lynched, and one reported that a lynching party had been organized at Columbia, but no report shows that he was harmed.

episodes.title: Steamer Dacotah killings
episodes.lead: The steamer Dacotah killings were an attack on Black deckhands aboard the Ohio River steamer Dacotah, laid up near Catlettsburg, Kentucky, in late November 1880, in which the second mate and four white crewmen killed two Black men and seriously wounded two others. The rest of the boat's twenty-two Black deckhands were driven off the boat, and the story ran in white newspapers from Maine to Nebraska as a "bloody riot."

episodes.title: Cromer's Store election-day attack
episodes.lead: The Cromer's Store election-day attack took place on November 2, 1880, when a mounted party of armed white men rode up to the polls at Cromer's Store in Newberry County, South Carolina, beat Black voters and fired into the crowd, killing Warren Williams. A coroner's jury found that Williams was killed by persons unknown, and no report of an arrest was found. Newberry papers blamed outsiders said to be from Laurens County and praised local whites for driving them off, while a Kansas Republican paper reprinted the account as proof of Southern election violence.

episodes.title: Shooting of Joseph Wills by a Richmond policeman
episodes.lead: The shooting of Joseph Wills was the wounding of a Black man by Richmond, Virginia, police officer Hulcher on November 22, 1880, during an arrest for the alleged theft of a pair of boots. Wills, who also went by William Jackson, was shot in the left leg, later sentenced to twenty-five lashes for the theft, and then pleaded guilty to resisting the officer.

episodes.title: Killing of William Towey
episodes.lead: The killing of William Towey was the fatal shooting of a Black man by two sheriff's deputies near Huntsville, Alabama, on November 26, 1880. According to a Huntsville dispatch, Deputy-Sheriff Cooper and Special Deputy W. J. Franks shot Towey while trying to arrest him, after he raised a shotgun at them. The brief item ran in Chicago and Omaha papers under headlines that called him a "desperado" and a "Desperate Darky."

episodes.title: Shooting of Willis Reed
episodes.lead: The shooting of Willis Reed took place at Columbus, Texas, on a Saturday night in late November 1880, probably 20 November, when officers trying to arrest Reed, a Black man, shot him three times. Reed was captured and handed to a doctor, who expected him to recover; the only known report is a short item in the Brenham Weekly Banner.

episodes.title: Ku Klux search of G. W. Witherspoon's house
episodes.lead: The Ku Klux search of G. W. Witherspoon's house was a night raid in Jefferson County, Florida, around the November 1880 election, in which a masked and armed band entered and searched the home of Witherspoon, a Black Republican candidate for Congress, just after he had been forced to leave it. Witherspoon was driven from his county, and no one was reported hurt. The episode became known through a New York Times correspondent who offered it as an example of election fraud and violence in Florida's "Black Belt."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Tom Hawkins
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Tom Hawkins took place in Mono County, California, in November 1880, when citizens of Bridgeport formed a Vigilance Committee to hang Hawkins, a gambler accused of shooting Henry Robbins on election day. Officials moved Hawkins to Bodie and then, after threats there, to Aurora, Nevada, and no report says he was harmed. The story ran in Nevada and California dailies as a short item in Bodie wire dispatches, and none of them stated the race of either man.

episodes.title: Pursuit of Andrew Beal
episodes.lead: The pursuit of Andrew Beal was a manhunt by white citizens near Franklin, Missouri, on December 25, 1880, for a young Black man accused of killing a railroad engineer, Henry Speers, with a razor the night before. The Chicago Tribune described the searchers as 'a Party of Lynchers' and predicted that Beal would disappear if caught, but no report of his capture or fate appeared.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Bruce at Dardanelle
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Bruce at Dardanelle took place on a Sunday night in December 1880, when a body of fifty men tried to take a prisoner named Bruce from his guards at the jail in Dardanelle, Arkansas, in order to lynch him. Prosecuting Attorney McKennon and the county officers intervened, and the attempt failed.

episodes.title: La Joya shooting and manhunt (1880)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The La Joya shooting and manhunt was a December 1880 episode in New Mexico Territory in which a storekeeper shot four Mexican men at La Joya and a sheriff's posse, later reported as thirty men, hunted him with open talk of lynching. Wire reports named the fugitive as Charles Bonssill or Bonsail, but the Las Vegas Morning Gazette later said the shooter was a Texan, John B. Hall, who escaped the country and so avoided a lynching.

episodes.title: Lynching of Charles Marshall
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Charles Marshall was the hanging of a former livery-stable hand by a band of armed men at Belleville, Esmeralda County, Nevada, in early December 1880. Marshall was accused of killing John (Jack) McCann, an older man who had replaced him at the stable, and was seized and hanged before any trial. A brief wire dispatch carried the story across the country, while Nevada papers printed fuller local accounts that contradicted the wire on how Marshall was taken.

episodes.title: Point Pleasant Christmas disturbance of 1880
episodes.lead: The Point Pleasant Christmas disturbance of 1880 was a day of drinking, street fighting and racial threats among crowds of white and Black men on Main Street in Point Pleasant, West Virginia, on December 25, 1880. Men on each side threatened to drive the other race from town and drew weapons, but no shot was fired and no one was arrested. The town's weekly paper called it a disgrace and urged arrests, the closing of saloons and, failing official action, a vigilance committee.

episodes.title: Socorro Committee of Safety hostage-taking (1880)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Socorro Committee of Safety hostage-taking was the armed seizure, on December 28, 1880, of the sheriff of Socorro, New Mexico Territory, his deputy and members of the Baca family by a citizens' committee seeking the alleged killers of newspaper editor A. M. Conklin. One hostage, Antonio Maria Baca, was shot dead under the committee's guard, and federal troops were sent to protect property. Newspapers framed the episode as a near 'war of races' between the town's American and Mexican residents.

episodes.title: Threatened expulsion of alleged cotton thieves in Oglethorpe County, Georgia
episodes.lead: The threatened expulsion of alleged cotton thieves in Oglethorpe County, Georgia, followed the capture in late 1880 of one of two Black men accused of stealing cotton from under George B. Lumpkin's gin house. According to the Oglethorpe Echo, indignant citizens intended to drive the whole alleged band of thieves out of the neighborhood, though no report shows that they did so. The Echo's paragraph circulated through Georgia exchange columns for two weeks in December.

episodes.title: Lynching of Dan Smith
episodes.lead: The lynching of Dan Smith took place on December 2, 1880, at Pulaski, Tennessee, when a crowd seized Smith, a Black man, from the Giles County courtroom minutes after he was sentenced to 21 years in the penitentiary and hanged him in the bridge over Richland Creek. Smith had pleaded guilty to assaulting a white girl with intent to rape, and the papers reported that the crowd acted because the law did not allow a death sentence for the offense. The Nashville wire carried the story to dailies across the country, while Tennessee papers defended the killing and at least one Ohio paper called it murder.

episodes.title: Lynching of C. A. Washington
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of C. A. Washington was the killing of a physician by a mob at Otero, New Mexico Territory, on the night of Thursday, December 2, 1880. Washington had been accused in the dying statement of a young hotel worker at Raton of drugging and assaulting her, and a mob that followed him from Raton took him from confinement and hanged him. Denver wire reports carried the story across the country, and Western papers presented the killing as deserved, while no report identified Washington as Black.

episodes.title: Smithville shooting (1880)
episodes.lead: The Smithville shooting took place on Christmas Eve, December 24, 1880, at Smithville, Virginia, a hamlet on the road between Hampton and Yorktown, when a white farmer named Howard Dunn shot two Black men dead and stabbed others at a gathering called to organize a Black military company. Dunn surrendered, was tried in March 1881, and was acquitted. The wire story ran in papers across the country, and a later letter from Yorktown called the trial a sham.

episodes.title: Killing of Garnett Thompson
episodes.lead: The killing of Garnett Thompson was the shooting death of a Black man by pursuers in Bayou Sara, West Feliciana Parish, Louisiana, on the evening of 11 December 1880, minutes after he shot a white man, J. C. Ball, in a street altercation. A coroner's jury found that he died from "shots fired by unknown hands," and the local paper gave particular attention to a claim that he was an escaped convicted murderer.

episodes.title: Lynching of George Scott
episodes.lead: The lynching of George Scott took place at Brazil, Indiana, on the night of December 11-12, 1880, when masked men took him from the jail and hanged him. Scott, described in the press as "a half-breed Indian and negro," was held on an accusation of assaulting Mrs. Allison, the wife of his employer. The story ran nationally as a short wire item, several papers headlined it approvingly, and a Texas editor used it to charge Northern papers with a double standard on lynching.

episodes.title: Lynching of Granville Harrell
episodes.lead: The lynching of Granville Harrell took place on the night of Saturday, December 18, 1880, when a mob took Harrell, a Black man accused of murdering his employer, from the Hinds County jail at Raymond, Mississippi, and hanged him to a tree outside the town. A coroner's jury found that unknown men had done it and cleared the sheriff and his deputies. Mississippi papers covered both the killing and the lynching at length, while the national wire ran it as a one-line item.

episodes.title: Police shooting at Henry Armistead
episodes.lead: The police shooting at Henry Armistead took place on the evening of December 4, 1880, on Harrison street in Chicago, when two officers fired at a young Black man accused of snatching a watch from a jewelry store. Neither shot hit him, and he was arrested and jailed; the Chicago Daily Tribune reported the episode the next morning as one item in its roundup of petty crime.

episodes.title: Lynching of James Anderson
episodes.lead: The lynching of James Anderson was the hanging of a Black man by a mob from a telegraph pole in front of the court house in Pine Bluff, Arkansas, on December 4, 1880. Anderson, accused of raping the wife of a Pine Bluff butcher and robbing her house that morning, was taken by force from the officers who had brought him back under arrest. Southern papers presented the hanging as "speedy justice", and wire summaries carried it to papers from Virginia to Kansas and Wyoming.

episodes.title: Killing of Jasper Vance
episodes.lead: The killing of Jasper Vance was the fatal shooting of a Black man by two deputy constables in the countryside near Rock Island, Arkansas, in December 1880, as they tried to arrest his wife. According to a wire dispatch, he swore they would take her only over his dead body and was shot in the fight that followed. The story ran as a short item in Chicago, Wheeling, Omaha and Watertown, Wisconsin, under headlines that cast him as a husband who died defending his wife.

episodes.title: Lynching of Joe Barnes, Vance Brandt and Julia Brandt
episodes.lead: The lynching of Joe Barnes, Vance Brandt and Julia Brandt was the hanging of three young Black people by a crowd near Salem, Clarendon County, South Carolina, on December 8, 1880. Accused of killing Ada Kennedy, a young white woman, at her home three days earlier, they were hanged near the spot after the crowd voted against holding them for court. Wire reports carried it nationally, and South Carolina papers defended it in editorials.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Fish
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of John Fish was an episode in Duke Centre, McKean County, Pennsylvania, reported in December 1880, in which a posse went to Fish's house intending to lynch him. Fish had already fled, and no one was harmed. The episode survives in a single paragraph of Pennsylvania state news, which does not give Fish's race.

episodes.title: Lynching of Joseph Snyder
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Joseph Snyder took place on December 27, 1880, at Santee's Mills near Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, when a crowd took Snyder, accused of murdering Jacob and Anna Gogel, from a detective and hanged him from a chestnut tree. Newspapers called it the first lynching ever to occur in Pennsylvania, and it drew editorial condemnation in New York and across the state. Warrants were reported, but a grand jury later declined to take up the case.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Major Hicks
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Major Hicks took place on the night of December 17, 1880, when an armed crowd from Ludlow, Kentucky, besieged the jail at Covington to seize Hicks, a Black youth held on suspicion of murdering a white railway worker. The city marshal's guard refused to give him up, a few shots were fired, and the crowd dispersed after midnight. Hicks was later tried, convicted and legally hanged at Covington in February 1882.

episodes.title: Lynching of Pantaleon Miera and Santos Benavides
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Pantaleon Miera and Santos Benavides was the hanging of two men at Bernalillo, New Mexico Territory, on the night of Tuesday, December 28, 1880. Later reports attributed Miera's death to vigilantes acting on an accusation of horse stealing. The case drew notice beyond the territory a month later, when Miera was named as one of the men who had killed Colonel Charles Potter of the U.S. Geological Survey.

episodes.title: Lynching of Alvin McKanna
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Alvin McKanna was the burning of a white lodger, known in the first reports as Miller, by a crowd of men in northern Monroe County, Mississippi, in December 1880. He was accused of chloroforming, robbing and burning to death a young farmer, his wife and their two-year-old daughter, and was killed at the scene of the fire after his capture. The case drew national wire coverage and an exchange of editorials between Northern and Southern papers over whether the burning was justice or murder.

episodes.title: Lynching of Alvin McKanna
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Alvin McKanna was the burning to death of a man accused of murder, robbery and arson by a crowd of local men in Bigby Fork, northern Monroe County, Mississippi, on December 18 or 19, 1880. McKanna, who had given the name Miller, was accused of helping to rob and kill William Brown Ridings, his wife and their young daughter and burning their house over them. Wire reports carried the story across the country as a crime of exceptional horror met with fitting retribution, and it drew editorial argument between Northern and Southern papers.

episodes.title: Lynching of Sam and John Campbell
episodes.lead: The lynching of Sam and John Campbell took place about midnight on December 23, 1880, when a crowd of seventy-five to one hundred men took the two Black brothers from the jail at Munfordville, Hart County, Kentucky, and hanged them from a tree below the town. The brothers had been arrested that day on suspicion of beating and robbing John A. Gardner, a magistrate described as one of the county's most prominent citizens. Wire dispatches carried the story to papers across the country within two days, and digests of it were still being printed in mid-January 1881.

episodes.title: Liberty vagrancy auction
episodes.lead: The Liberty vagrancy auction was the public sale of three Black people at Liberty, Bedford County, Virginia, on December 13, 1880, under an old state vagrancy law, by order of a magistrate. The buyers paid about $4 apiece for a term of up to three months, and a county judge freed the three on habeas corpus within days. Papers across the country carried the story, some as a sign of slavery's return and others as a joke about falling prices.

episodes.title: Burning of the Smith and Brisco store, Grant Parish, Louisiana
episodes.lead: The burning of the Smith and Brisco store was the destruction by fire of a store owned by two Black men, Israel Smith and Hansom Brisco, eight or ten miles southeast of Colfax in Grant Parish, Louisiana, on the night of December 9, 1880. No one was hurt, but the local paper first described it as an attack by armed "incendiaries" and then, a week later, reported a rumor that the owners had burned the store themselves for the insurance.

episodes.title: Killing of Wright in Sumter County, South Carolina
episodes.lead: The killing of Wright was the fatal shooting of a Black man named Wright by a deputy in Sumter County, South Carolina, on December 30, 1880, while deputies tried to arrest him on a charge of stealing a bale of cotton. A Charleston dispatch said Wright had cut and shot Deputy Sheriff Bateman before he was killed, and a coroner's jury later returned a verdict of "justifiable homicide."

episodes.title: Lynching of a gambler in a Colorado mining town (1880)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of a gambler in a Colorado mining town was the hanging of a man called 'Jim', accused of shooting a police officer, by fifteen or twenty miners who took him from the town lock-up in 1880. It is known chiefly from the account of a Pittsburgh oil inspector named Ramsey, who said he watched it, and whose story ran in eastern papers in late 1880. His details closely match a lynching at Kokomo, near Leadville, reported in July 1880, though no paper said the two were the same.

episodes.title: Threats against exodus leader Samuel L. Perry
episodes.lead: The threats against exodus leader Samuel L. Perry were a series of warnings and a search by armed horsemen aimed at Perry, a Black teacher and organizer, at Lagrange, Lenoir County, North Carolina, in late 1879, after he led Black emigrants from the state to Indiana. No attack on him is reported; the episode became public in November 1880, when Perry's wife and mother described it under oath in Washington while he fought extradition to North Carolina on a forgery charge.

episodes.title: Alleged lynching of a Swiss settler on Loup Creek, West Virginia (1880)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The alleged lynching of a Swiss settler on Loup Creek was a claim, printed in German-language papers in 1880, that local whites in West Virginia's Kanawha Valley had threatened or lynched a Swiss immigrant for making his wife work. The man, identified as David Braun, was reported alive and prosperous in November 1880 and denied that any lynching had occurred. West Virginia papers treated the story as a slander meant to stop Swiss immigration to the state.
